newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Outcast Bryant haunts Port Arthur site.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Outcast Bryant haunts Port Arthur site.

text.p: One year on, flowers lie where blood was spilt around the clipped lawns of Port Arthur.
Scattered among the ruins of one of Australia's most brutal penal colonies, simple bouquets and wreaths mark the ground where 35 people died on April 28.
Ever since the first petal kissed the blood-stained earth there 12 months ago, the flowers have been gathered up, stored and allowed to rot.
"It's nearly a shed-full now," said an emotional Craig Coombs, chief executive of the Port Arthur Historic Site where a a young social misfit, Martin Bryant, opened fire on tourists.
MEMORIAL GARDEN
The composted flowers will be used eventually to establish a memorial garden of 30,000 or more daffodils at the site, a riot of yellow to be planted near the tourist site's old cafe.
It was inside the brick-built Broad Arrow Cafe, now itself in ruins, that modern Australia's worst mass murder exploded.

As 60 tourists ate their lunch on a crisp autumn Sunday afternoon, Bryant, then aged 28, got up from his own meal, took a semi-automatic rifle from his sports bag and calmly walked from table to table shooting at point blank range, laughing as he went.
Within 15 seconds, 12 people were dead; within two minutes, 20. Later, the body of Malaysian tourist Moh Yee William Ng, among the first shot, was found still clutching a dinner knife.
The carnage continued outside the cafe, as Bryant hunted down victims at random, waving his semi-automatic rifle around in a manner many tourists mistook for a historical re-enactment.

Tragically, a mother and her two daughters, aged three and six, later mistook Bryant for a tourist fleeing the site in his car. Bryant slowed his Volvo as Nanette Mikac and her daughters approached hurriedly on foot, begging for a lift.
He got out of the car and shot them. Six-year-old Alannah had run behind a tree when Bryant put the gun to her neck.

Recently, three small homemade crosses appeared on the grassy slope where Nanette, Madeline and Alannah died. They were planted there by Nanette's husband, Walter, and represent the loss of his entire family.
"I feel a bit numb, angry, a litte bit angry, that's really about as far as I've let myself go," Mikac told reporters last week, as the news media began to focus again on Port Arthur.
"Really, all I can think about is that I'm in a dream. It's really hard to comprehend that what's happened here has happened."
NIGHTMARE RELIVED

The nightmare of Port Arthur has again become a vivid and recurring one for the family of the dead and survivors as the first anniversary nears. Wounds beginning to heal are picked open and brave faces become masks of grief.
"I am not looking forward to Monday at all," said the Port Arthur site's Coombs, who saw the full horror left behind at the Broad Arrow Cafe.
"To date I've been able to keep my guard up, but I can feel a lump build up in my throat today even. I'm finding it more and more difficult to talk about the events of April 28."
Of the 22 Port Arthur staff on duty that day, about half have returned to their old jobs over the past 12 months.
Some had even felt able to talk about the massacre with visitors, but in recent days the anniversary has brought on another wave of flowers and with them more tears and grief.
Many staff have felt too distressed to go to work in recent days, leaving the site struggling to stay open.
On Monday, the victims of the massacre will be remembered with a memorial service inside the ruins of Port Arthur church.
BRYANT RELISHES ATTENTION
Jailed for life without parole, Bryant, now 29, relishes the attention his crime has brought him, according to psychologists who assessed his mental state before he was sentenced last year.
Bryant suffers a rare illness which renders him incapable of empathising with others yet paradoxically, as a loner with the mental age of a child, he craves companionship, they say.
An outcast, he also nursed a grudge against society.
"That combination is a very, very deadly and dangerous combination of factors," said forensic psychologist Ian Joblin.
Bryant will spend Monday like any other -- confined to his high-security suicide-proof cell in the Tasmanian capital, Hobart. But he will haunt the memorial service at Port Arthur.
Apart from Bryant, the loneliest person on Monday could well be his mother, Carleen Bryant, who said in a statement read on national radio she would shed her own bitter tears that day.
"Of all people I weep with you, with your bitter tears, with our suffering tears, with unique unsharable tears of my own," she said in a statement issued by her son's former lawyer.
